name: ai
purpose: The single door through which every LLM call passes. Business code asks for an **AI task** by name; this module decides which provider and model serve it, renders the versioned prompt, enforces quota and budget, caches, retries, falls back, validates the structured output, and records cost and usage.
context: No other module may import a provider SDK (rule: `AGENT.md` §10). That rule is what makes the model choice a configuration decision instead of a code change, and what makes cost, quality and safety controllable in one place.
businessPurpose: AI grading is the product's differentiator and its largest variable cost. Both facts demand that model routing, spend, and output quality be governed centrally and measurably rather than scattered through feature code.
responsibilities: Provider registry and adapters (anthropic, openai, gemini, openrouter, local, mock)
Task routing: task → model tier → concrete model, from configuration
Prompt registry: versioned templates with typed input and output schemas
Resilience: timeout, retry with backoff, circuit breaker, provider fallback chain
Caching: exact-hash and semantic (pgvector) with per-task policy
Quota (per user) and budget (global daily) enforcement
PII redaction before send and untrusted-content wrapping
Structured output validation, one repair attempt, and sanity bounds
Streaming (SSE) with partial persistence
Usage, cost, latency and quality metrics; the `ai_requests` / `ai_usage` audit trail
The evaluation harness that gates prompt changes
notResponsibilities: Deciding what a good essay score is — the rubric belongs to `writing`
Storing a graded submission — that is the calling module's data
Speech recognition or synthesis — that is `platform/media`
Choosing when to call an LLM — see `/AI_GUIDE.md` §B2 before you do

tables.name: ai_requests
tables.notes: Partitioned monthly. `task`, `prompt_version`, `provider`, `model`, `status`, `attempt`, `fallback_from`, `cache_hit`, `latency_ms`, `trace_id`. Request/response bodies redacted and retained 30 days.

tables.name: ai_usage
tables.notes: `user_id`, `task`, `tokens_in`, `tokens_out`, `cost_usd`, `occurred_on` — the source for per-user unit economics

endpoints.purpose: Spend and volume by task, provider and day

endpoints.notes: Bodies are redacted; full content requires `ai.read.sensitive` and is itself audited

endpoints.purpose: Deployed prompt versions and their status

contract.name: ai.Client
contract.purpose: `Run(ctx, TaskRequest) (TaskResult, error)` and `Stream(ctx, TaskRequest) (iter, error)` — the only surface business code touches

contract.name: ai.TaskRequest
contract.purpose: `{Task, Input (typed), UserID, Locale, IdempotencyKey}` — never a model name, never a raw prompt

contract.name: ai.TaskResult
contract.purpose: `{Output (validated JSON), Provider, Model, PromptVersion, Tokens, CostUSD, CacheHit}`

contract.name: ai.Provider
contract.purpose: The Strategy interface each adapter implements — internal, not for business code

dependsWhy.cache: Response cache, quota counters, provider circuit state
dependsWhy.telemetry: Spans and metrics on every call
dependsWhy.job: Long-running calls execute inside jobs; evals run on a schedule

rules: Business code names a **task**, never a model or a provider. A task not present in the routing config is a startup error, not a runtime surprise.
Prompts are loaded from `docs/prompts/runtime/<task>/v<N>.md`; a published version is immutable, and the active version is pinned by configuration.
Learner-supplied text is inserted only inside the untrusted-content wrapper; it is never concatenated into the instruction block.
Output must validate against the task's JSON schema. One repair attempt is allowed; a second failure fails the call with `AI_OUTPUT_INVALID`.
Numeric outputs are clamped to the rubric's range and cross-checked for internal consistency before being returned.
Every call checks the per-user quota and the global daily budget first; exceeding either fails fast without contacting a provider.
Retries apply only to 429, 5xx and timeouts. A refusal, a schema failure, or a content-policy rejection is not retried against the same provider.
When a provider's circuit is open, the next provider in the task's fallback chain is used and the substitution is recorded.
No call blocks an HTTP request for more than 2 seconds; anything longer runs in a job and streams or notifies.
Every call writes `ai_requests` and `ai_usage`, including cache hits and failures — otherwise cost attribution has holes.
In tests, the `mock` provider is used. Unit and integration tests never reach a network.
A prompt version cannot be activated unless its eval suite meets its thresholds and is no worse than the currently active version.

cache.ttl: until midnight in the user's timezone

errors.meaning: Global daily spend cap reached; non-critical tasks are shed first
Every provider in the chain failed
Output failed schema validation after the repair attempt
Prompt promotion blocked by its eval suite

security: Provider API keys live in configuration only and never appear in a span, a log, or an error.
PII redaction runs before send; the redaction map is retained only long enough to restore names in the response.
Only providers contractually barred from training on API data receive learner content; `openrouter` is restricted to non-personal input.
The untrusted-content wrapper plus a hardened system preamble is the primary prompt-injection defence; the eval suite includes a red-team subset that must score 1.0.
Score sanity bounds are the second line of defence: an out-of-range or internally inconsistent score fails the job rather than reaching the learner.

flows.title: A task call, end to end
flows.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["ai.Client.Run(task, input)"] --> B{Task in routing config?}
    B -->|no| Z1[startup error — cannot happen at runtime]
    B -->|yes| C{User opted out?}
    C -->|yes| Z2[AI_OPTED_OUT]
    C -->|no| D{Quota + budget OK?}
    D -->|no| Z3[AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED / AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED]
    D -->|yes| E[Redact PII]
    E --> F[Wrap untrusted content]
    F --> G[Render prompt vN]
    G --> H{Cache hit?}
    H -->|exact| I[Return cached + record usage]
    H -->|semantic within threshold| I
    H -->|miss| J[Provider 1 via breaker]
    J -->|429/5xx/timeout| K{Retries left?}
    K -->|yes| J
    K -->|no| L{Next provider?}
    L -->|yes| J
    L -->|no| Z4[AI_UNAVAILABLE]
    J -->|response| M[Validate against output schema]
    M -->|invalid| N[One repair attempt]
    N -->|still invalid| Z5[AI_OUTPUT_INVALID]
    M -->|valid| O[Clamp + consistency check]
    O -->|out of bounds| Z5
    O --> P[Cache, record ai_requests + ai_usage, emit metrics]
    P --> Q[Return TaskResult]

flows.title: Provider fallback
flows.description: Fallback is per task, not global — a cheap task may have no fallback at all, while grading has two.
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Caller
    participant R as Resilience chain
    participant P1 as anthropic
    participant P2 as openai
    participant M as Metrics

    C->>R: Run(writing.grade_essay)
    R->>P1: request (timeout 30s)
    P1-->>R: 503
    R->>R: retry 1 after 1s ± jitter
    R->>P1: request
    P1-->>R: 503
    R->>R: breaker opens for anthropic
    R->>M: ai_provider_degraded, ai_fallback_total
    R->>P2: request with the same rendered prompt
    P2-->>R: 200
    R->>M: record provider=openai, fallback_from=anthropic
    R-->>C: TaskResult

stateMachine.description: Prompt version lifecycle. A version never returns to an earlier state; rollback means activating the previous version, not editing this one.
stateMachine.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft: author vN+1
    Draft --> Shadow: eval thresholds met + human approval
    Shadow --> Draft: comparison worse
    Shadow --> Rollout10: shadow results acceptable
    Rollout10 --> Active: metrics stable
    Rollout10 --> Draft: regression detected
    Active --> Deprecated: superseded by vN+2
    Deprecated --> [*]

failures.behaviour: Job retries with backoff; the learner sees "still grading", not an error; pages after 5 minutes

failures.failure: Provider silently changes a model behind an alias
failures.behaviour: Alert; models are pinned to exact IDs to make this rare

failures.failure: Schema violations spike after a prompt change
failures.behaviour: Automatic rollback to the previous active version at > 5 % over 30 minutes
80 % budget alert; at 100 % non-critical tasks are shed while grading continues

tasks.title: Add a provider
steps: Create `provider/<name>/` implementing `ai.Provider`. The vendor SDK may be imported **only** inside this directory.
Map vendor errors onto the module's retryable/non-retryable classification.
Add config keys and register the provider in the registry.
Add `mock` fixtures so tests covering this provider stay offline.
Add it to the fallback chains that should use it, in config.
Run the eval suites against it and record the results in `docs/ai/provider-comparison.md`.

tasks.title: Add an AI task
steps: Follow the checklist in `/AI_GUIDE.md` §B4 — it is the authoritative list.
Define the task in the routing config with tier, timeout, cache policy and budget.
Write `docs/prompts/runtime/<task>/v1.md` plus input and output schemas.
Build the golden set (≥ 30 examples) and `thresholds.yaml`, including red-team cases.
Add `mock` fixtures.
Call it from the owning module by task name only.

tasks.title: Change the model for a task
steps: Edit the routing config — **do not touch Go code**.
Run the eval suite; compare cost and quality deltas.
Shadow, then 10 %, then 100 %.
Record the change and its measured effect in `docs/ai/cost-model.md`.

limitations: Semantic caching depends on `pgvector` and an embedding call, which itself costs money — it is enabled only for tasks where the hit rate justifies it.
The repair attempt is a single retry with the validation error appended; there is no multi-turn negotiation.
Streaming partials are persisted per chunk, which is chatty for long outputs.
Cost figures are computed from a published price table in config and can drift from actual invoices; monthly reconciliation is manual.
conventions: No prompt string literal anywhere in Go code.
Every provider adapter has a `mock` fixture set covering success, refusal, timeout, rate limit and malformed output.
testFocus: Fallback chain: killing provider 1 must produce a correct result from provider 2 with the substitution recorded
Quota and budget enforcement, including the boundary at exactly the cap
Schema validation and the single repair attempt
Score clamping and consistency checks reject an out-of-range score
Prompt injection: red-team fixtures must not change the output score
Cache correctness: a different input must never return a cached response
Cost accounting matches the token counts reported by the provider
Streaming: a disconnect mid-stream does not lose already-generated content
testEdges: Two identical requests arriving concurrently — single-flight must produce one provider call
A provider returning valid JSON that violates the schema in a subtle way (extra field, wrong enum)
An empty submission, a 10,000-word submission, and one that is entirely emoji

decisions.question: Task-based or model-based API?
decisions.why: Callers should not know or care which model runs; it makes model changes a config decision, keeps routing and cost policy in one place, and makes the eval story coherent

decisions.question: Where do prompts live?
decisions.why: Reviewable by non-engineers, diffable, evaluable in CI, rollback-able by config — none of which is true of a Go string constant

decisions.question: Fail open or closed on budget exhaustion?
decisions.why: A learner who paid for grading should still get it; example-sentence generation can wait

decisions.question: Semantic cache everywhere?
decisions.choice: Only where measured hit rate justifies the embedding cost
decisions.why: An embedding call to save a small-model call can be a net loss

openQuestions: Do we self-host a small model for high-volume cheap tasks once volume justifies it?
Should the semantic cache be per-user or global for privacy-sensitive tasks?

doNot: Do not import a provider SDK outside `provider/<name>/`.
Do not name a model in business code — name a task.
Do not inline a prompt string.
Do not call an LLM synchronously in an HTTP handler for anything expected to take more than 2 seconds.
Do not trust model output — validate the schema, clamp the numbers, check the consistency.
Do not concatenate learner text into the instruction block.
Do not skip the eval suite because "it's a small prompt change". That is exactly when regressions slip through.
Do not use an LLM where an algorithm exists — read `/AI_GUIDE.md` §B2 first.

runtimePrompts.purpose: CEFR/IELTS rubric grading with actionable feedback
Turn ASR output and pronunciation scores into coaching
Explain an error, citing a rule from our own taxonomy
Estimate the CEFR level of a passage

name: media
purpose: Everything that happens to audio and images: transcoding, waveform generation, speech recognition, pronunciation assessment, text-to-speech, and thumbnailing. It is the CPU-heavy part of the system and the first candidate for extraction to a separate service.
businessPurpose: Listening and speaking are half the product. Neither works without a reliable pipeline that turns a learner's browser recording into something a scoring engine can read, and turns published text into natural audio.
responsibilities: Audio transcoding (ffmpeg) to canonical formats: 16 kHz mono for ASR, Opus for playback
Waveform peak extraction for the player UI
ASR adapter: transcript plus word-level timings
Pronunciation assessment adapter: phoneme-level accuracy, fluency, completeness
Text-to-speech adapter with voice selection and caching
Image processing: resize, EXIF strip, re-encode, thumbnail
Duration, format and loudness validation
Orphaned-derivative garbage collection
notResponsibilities: Deciding what a pronunciation score means for a learner — that is `speaking`

tables.name: media_derivatives
tables.purpose: Derived artefacts from a source asset

tables.name: tts_cache
tables.purpose: Synthesised audio keyed by text and voice

endpoints.purpose: Inspect the pipeline output for one asset

contract.name: media.Processor
contract.purpose: `Transcode`, `Waveform`, `Thumbnail` — enqueue-and-return, never synchronous

contract.name: media.Recognizer
contract.purpose: `Transcribe(ctx, assetID, lang)` → transcript with word timings

contract.name: media.Assessor
contract.purpose: `AssessPronunciation(ctx, assetID, referenceText)` → phoneme-level scores

contract.name: media.Synthesizer
contract.purpose: `Speak(ctx, text, voice)` → an asset ID, cached by text and voice

consumes.name: content.published
consumes.reason: Pre-generate TTS for newly published text

dependsWhy.job: Every stage runs as a job — none is fast enough for a request
dependsWhy.ai: Post-processing of transcripts into feedback is an AI task, invoked by the calling module

rules: No media processing happens in the API process. Every stage is a job on the `media` queue.
Source files are never mutated; every output is a new derivative with its own object key.
ASR receives 16 kHz mono PCM — always transcode first, never send the browser's original.
Uploads are validated for real content type by magic bytes, not by extension or the declared MIME type.
Maximum recording length is 180 seconds; maximum upload 25 MB. Both are configuration, enforced server-side after upload as well as in the presigned URL.
TTS output is cached by (text hash, voice, model); the same sentence is never synthesised twice.
A failed stage retries up to 3 times, then records `media.processing_failed` with a user-safe reason.
Raw user uploads are deleted once derivatives exist and are verified; only the normalised versions are retained.
Every derivative records the exact tool version used, so a pipeline change can be correlated with a quality change.

errors.meaning: Magic bytes do not match a supported container
A pipeline stage failed after retries
Audio too noisy or too quiet to score fairly

security: Uploads land in a private quarantine bucket and are never publicly readable, even transiently.
Content type is verified by sniffing before ffmpeg is invoked.
ffmpeg runs with a wall-clock limit and a memory cap; a malformed file must not be able to exhaust the worker.
Voice recordings are personal data: 90-day retention, deletable by the learner, and never sent to a provider without no-training terms.

flows.title: Speaking attempt pipeline
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant J as job queue
    participant W as worker (media)
    participant S as storage
    participant F as ffmpeg
    participant A as ASR provider
    participant P as pronunciation provider

    J->>W: speaking.transcribe_and_score { asset_id }
    W->>S: GET raw upload
    W->>W: sniff magic bytes, probe duration
    alt invalid or too long
        W->>W: fail with a user-safe reason
    else valid
        W->>F: transcode → 16 kHz mono WAV
        W->>F: transcode → 64 kbps Opus (playback)
        W->>F: extract waveform peaks
        W->>S: PUT derivatives
        W->>A: transcribe (16 kHz WAV)
        A-->>W: transcript + word timings + confidence
        alt confidence below threshold
            W->>W: TRANSCRIPTION_LOW_CONFIDENCE — ask the learner to re-record
        else
            W->>P: assess against the reference text
            P-->>W: phoneme accuracy, fluency, completeness
            W->>W: persist transcript + scores; publish media.transcribed
            W->>S: DELETE raw upload
        end
    end

tasks.title: Add a media stage
steps: Add the job kind and register the worker in `job/`.
Make it idempotent — a re-run must produce the same derivative key.
Add per-stage duration and failure metrics.
Add resource limits (time, memory) to the external tool invocation.
Cover it with an integration test using a small real audio fixture, not a synthetic buffer.

tasks.title: Swap the ASR provider
steps: Implement `media.Recognizer` in a new adapter directory.
Run the benchmark suite in `test/fixtures/corpus/speech/` and compare word error rate and cost.
Record the comparison in `docs/knowledge/pronunciation-scoring.md`.
Switch by configuration; keep the previous adapter for one release.

limitations: ffmpeg runs in-process in the worker container; a single very large file can occupy a worker slot for minutes.
Pronunciation assessment quality varies by accent and is weakest for non-native reference speakers — documented for the product team.
There is no forced-alignment fallback if the ASR provider does not return word timings.
TTS voice selection is per-locale, not per-learner.
testFocus: Magic-byte sniffing rejects a renamed file
Duration and size limits enforced after upload, not only in the presigned URL
Idempotent reprocessing produces identical derivative keys
Low-confidence transcripts are surfaced rather than scored
Raw uploads are deleted only after derivatives are verified present
TTS cache prevents duplicate synthesis
coverage: 80% service; integration tests carry the pipeline

decisions.question: ffmpeg in the worker or a separate service?
decisions.why: One fewer moving part; the boundary is already an interface, so extraction is a transport change when CPU contention justifies it — see ARCHITECTURE §20.2 where media is the first extraction candidate

decisions.question: Which pronunciation scoring approach?
decisions.choice: Provider API first, GOP self-hosted as a fallback option
decisions.why: Building phoneme-level scoring in-house is a research project; buying it lets us ship and measure. Open question Q2 in the plan review

decisions.question: Keep raw uploads?
decisions.why: Storage cost and privacy; the normalised copy is what any re-scoring would use anyway

name: job
purpose: Background execution: the River queue wiring, the cron scheduler, job middleware (tracing, logging, panic recovery, timeouts), the dead-letter path, and the operational surface for inspecting and retrying work.
context: Jobs are enqueued **inside the business transaction**, so a job can never exist for a row that was rolled back, and a row can never exist without its follow-up work. That single property is why River was chosen over a Redis queue (ADR-0010).
responsibilities: River client and worker wiring, queue registry, concurrency configuration
Cron scheduling with distributed locking
Job middleware: span, structured log, panic recovery, timeout, metrics
Retry policy and dead-letter handling
The outbox publisher loop
Queue depth and age metrics
Admin operations: inspect, retry, cancel
notResponsibilities: The business logic inside a job — that lives in the owning module's `job/` package
Deciding retry semantics for a business failure — the module classifies its own errors

tables.name: river_job
tables.notes: Managed by River's own migrations; do not hand-edit. Applied by `job.MigrateUp` at worker start-up, **not** by goose — River versions this schema itself, so it is deliberately absent from `db/migrations/job/`

tables.name: outbox_events
tables.notes: `aggregate`, `event`, `payload`, `published_at`, `attempts`. Polled with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`; published, non-dead-lettered rows are deleted daily after `OUTBOX_PUBLISHED_RETENTION_DAYS` (30 by default).

endpoints.purpose: List jobs by queue and state
Depth, oldest pending age, throughput per queue

contract.name: job.Enqueuer
contract.purpose: `Enqueue(ctx, tx, args)` — takes the transaction, which is the whole point

contract.name: job.Scheduler
contract.purpose: `Register(spec, kind)` for cron entries

contract.name: job.Meta
contract.purpose: `{TraceID, RequestID, UserID}` carried in every job payload for correlation

dependsWhy.telemetry: Every job is a span; every queue is metered

rules: Enqueue inside the transaction that creates the data the job will read. Never after commit.
Every job handler is idempotent — delivery is at-least-once and a retry must be safe.
Job arguments carry IDs, never payloads. The handler re-reads current state; stale embedded data causes subtle bugs.
Every job declares a timeout and a maximum attempt count.
A business rejection is not retried; only transient failures are.
Every job carries `trace_id` and `request_id` so its logs join the originating request's trace.
Cron handlers must tolerate double execution — distributed locking reduces the chance but does not eliminate it.
A permanently failed job writes to `job_failures` and emits an event; it never disappears silently.
Queues are isolated by workload: `ai`, `media`, `notify`, `batch`, `default`. A slow media job must not starve notifications.

errors.meaning: Admin attempted to retry a job that failed for a business reason

flows.title: Transactional enqueue and the outbox
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as Service
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant OB as Outbox publisher
    participant W as Worker

    S->>DB: BEGIN
    S->>DB: INSERT business row
    S->>DB: INSERT river_job (same tx)
    S->>DB: INSERT outbox_events (same tx)
    S->>DB: COMMIT
    Note over S,DB: all three commit atomically — no orphans, no lost work
    W->>DB: dequeue job (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
    W->>W: run handler inside span + timeout
    alt transient failure
        W->>DB: reschedule with exponential backoff
    else business failure
        W->>DB: INSERT job_failures; publish job.failed_permanently
    else success
        W->>DB: mark completed
    end
    OB->>DB: poll unpublished outbox rows
    OB->>OB: dispatch to in-process subscribers
    OB->>DB: mark published

tasks.title: Add a job kind
steps: Define the args struct in the owning module's `job/` package; include only IDs plus `job.Meta`.
Implement the worker; make it idempotent and re-read state.
Register it in `cmd/worker`.
Choose a queue, timeout and attempt count deliberately.
Enqueue it inside the business transaction.
Add a test that runs the handler twice and asserts the same end state.

tasks.title: Add a scheduled task
steps: Register the cron spec in `cmd/worker`.
Make the handler idempotent and safe if it runs twice or is skipped once.
Use an advisory lock if it must not run concurrently across replicas.
Add a metric for its last successful run, and an alert if it goes stale.

limitations: Throughput is bounded by Postgres — comfortable to a few thousand jobs per second, far above our projection, but not a stream processor.
Jobs add write load to the primary database.
There is no priority within a queue beyond scheduled time; priority is expressed by using a different queue.
testFocus: Rollback of the business transaction leaves no job
Handler idempotency: running twice yields one effect
Retry backoff and the maximum-attempt boundary
Timeout cancels the handler's context
Panic in a handler is recovered and recorded, not fatal to the worker
Outbox publishes exactly once per event to each subscriber
Outbox retention deletes only published, non-dead-lettered rows past the configured window

decisions.question: River, Asynq, or a broker?
decisions.why: Transactional enqueue is worth more to us than raw throughput; see the comparison in ARCHITECTURE §11.1 and ADR-0010

decisions.question: Job args: IDs or full payloads?
decisions.why: A payload captured at enqueue time is stale by the time the job runs; re-reading is correct and keeps the queue table small

decisions.question: One queue or several?
decisions.why: A three-minute transcode must not delay a notification; separate queues give independent concurrency and independent alerting

decisions.question: Run cron jobs once at startup?
decisions.why: A fresh deployment otherwise waits out a whole interval doing nothing, which is an hour for upload verification. The advisory lock still stops two instances colliding, and the orchestrator's restart backoff bounds how often a crash-loop can repeat the call

name: cache
purpose: A typed facade over Redis: key building, serialisation, TTL policy, single-flight, distributed locks, and rate limiting. Modules never touch the Redis client directly, so key conventions and degradation behaviour are enforced in one place.
responsibilities: Typed get/set/delete with a generic `Cache[T]`
Key construction following the repository convention, including schema versioning
Cache-aside and write-through helpers
Single-flight to prevent stampedes
Jittered TTLs
Distributed locks (`SET NX PX`) with safe release
Rate limiting (GCRA via `redis_rate`)
Graceful degradation when Redis is unavailable
Hit-ratio and latency metrics per module
notResponsibilities: Deciding what to cache — each module owns that decision
Being a source of truth for anything except rate-limit counters and token denylists

endpoints.notes: Prefix-scoped and audited; never a bare `KEYS *`

contract.name: cache.Cache[T]
contract.purpose: `Get`, `Set`, `Delete`, `GetOrLoad` — typed, so a cached value cannot be deserialised into the wrong shape

contract.name: cache.Locker
contract.purpose: `Acquire(ctx, key, ttl)` returning a release function

contract.name: cache.Limiter
contract.purpose: `Allow(ctx, key, limit)` returning remaining and reset

contract.name: cache.Key
contract.purpose: Builds `fluentra:{env}:{module}:{entity}:{id}:v{n}` — the only sanctioned way to make a key

rules: Every read path must work with Redis down: fall back to the source, log at `warn`, increment `cache_unavailable_total`. A cache outage degrades latency, never correctness.
Keys are built only via `cache.Key`. A hand-built key string fails review.
Every cached class carries a schema version; bumping it invalidates the whole class without scanning.
TTLs carry ±10 % jitter to avoid synchronised expiry.
`GetOrLoad` uses single-flight so a cold key produces one loader call, not a thundering herd.
Authorization decisions are never cached across users.
Personal data in the cache carries the same retention expectations as the database — deletion must bust the key.
Locks always have a TTL and are released with a token check, so a slow holder cannot release someone else's lock.

flows.title: Cache-aside with single-flight and degradation
flows.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["GetOrLoad(key, loader)"] --> B{Redis reachable?} B -->|no| L[call loader directly
warn + cache_unavailable_total] B -->|yes| C[GET key] C -->|hit| D[deserialise → return
cache_requests_total result=hit] C -->|miss| E[single-flight per key] E --> F[loader] F -->|error| G[return error, cache nothing] F -->|value| H[SET with jittered TTL] H --> I[return value

tasks.title: Cache a read path
steps: Confirm it is worth it: measure the underlying query first. Caching a 3 ms query buys nothing and adds an invalidation bug.
Choose the key shape and register it in your module's AGENT.md §Cache strategy.
Decide the invalidation trigger before writing the read — an uninvalidated cache is a correctness bug waiting.
Use `GetOrLoad`, not manual get/set.
Add a test proving the fallback path works with Redis unavailable.

limitations: Single Redis instance — no cluster in v1. A failure degrades every module simultaneously, which is why degradation is mandatory rather than optional.
No cache warming; cold starts hit the database.
Prefix invalidation uses `SCAN`, which is fine at our key counts but is not free.
testFocus: Every consumer's fallback path with Redis stopped
Single-flight collapses concurrent loads into one
TTL jitter is applied
Lock release is token-checked
Rate limiter boundaries: exactly at the limit, and just over
Version bump invalidates a whole class

decisions.question: go-redis or rueidis?
decisions.why: Maturity and instrumentation; rueidis is faster and supports client-side caching — revisit if Redis latency becomes a measured problem

decisions.question: Typed facade or raw client?
decisions.why: It is the only way to enforce key conventions, degradation and metrics consistently; a raw client in 20 modules produces 20 conventions

todo.title: Phase 1
items: Typed `Cache[T]` with JSON and msgpack codecs
`cache.Key` builder with environment and version segments

future: Two-tier cache with an in-process L1
Redis Cluster or Valkey if licensing or scale demands
Cache warming for the daily review queue
doNot: Do not build a key by string concatenation.
Do not treat the cache as a source of truth (except rate limits and denylists).
Do not cache without deciding how it is invalidated.
Do not cache a permission decision across users.
Do not use `KEYS` — ever.

name: storage
purpose: A facade over MinIO (S3 API): bucket policy, presigned upload and download URLs, object verification, lifecycle rules, and orphan collection. Binary data never flows through the Go API — this module is how that rule is kept.
responsibilities: Bucket definitions, policies and lifecycle rules
Presigned PUT (upload) and GET (download) with pinned content type, size and expiry
Post-upload verification: existence, size, content type
Object key conventions
Copy, move and delete operations
Orphan garbage collection
Storage metrics per bucket
notResponsibilities: Deciding who may access an object — the calling module authorises before requesting a URL

endpoints.purpose: Object counts and sizes per bucket

contract.name: storage.Store
contract.purpose: `PresignPut`, `PresignGet`, `Stat`, `Copy`, `Delete`

contract.name: storage.UploadIntent
contract.purpose: `{URL, ObjectKey, ExpiresAt, MaxBytes, ContentType}`

rules: Binary data never passes through the API process. Uploads and downloads use presigned URLs.
A presigned PUT pins content type and maximum size and expires in 5 minutes.
A presigned GET for private content expires in 15 minutes and is generated per request, never cached in a response the browser stores.
After an upload the server verifies existence, size and sniffed content type before accepting the reference.
Object keys are deterministic: `{bucket}/{owner_type}/{owner_id}/{yyyy}/{mm}/{asset_id}.{ext}` — so an orphan is identifiable and a re-run is idempotent.
Public buckets contain only published content; user uploads are always private.
Lifecycle rules enforce the retention table in ARCHITECTURE §8.5; retention is configuration, not a cron script.
An object without a database reference for more than 24 hours is collected by the GC job.

errors.meaning: The uploaded object does not match the intent

security: Buckets are private by default; making one public requires an explicit policy and a review.
Presigned URLs are the only access path; the application never proxies object bytes.
Access and secret keys are configuration only, scoped to the minimum bucket set.
Export and report artefacts are single-use in practice: short expiry plus an unguessable key.

flows.title: Presigned upload with verification
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor B as Browser
    participant A as API (calling module)
    participant ST as storage
    participant M as MinIO

    B->>A: POST …/upload-intent { content_type, size }
    A->>A: authorise + quota check
    A->>ST: PresignPut(bucket, key, 5m, max_bytes, content_type)
    ST->>M: sign
    ST-->>A: UploadIntent
    A-->>B: { upload_url, asset_id }
    B->>M: PUT bytes directly
    B->>A: POST …/confirm { asset_id }
    A->>ST: Stat(key)
    alt missing, wrong size, or wrong type
        A-->>B: 422 UPLOAD_VERIFICATION_FAILED
    else ok
        A->>A: mark asset uploaded; enqueue processing
        A-->>B: 202
    end

tasks.title: Add a bucket
steps: Define it in `deploy/minio/` with its policy and lifecycle rule.
Add the config key and the key-prefix convention.
Decide retention and add it to the retention table in ARCHITECTURE §8.5.
Include it in the GC job and in the storage metrics.
Document who may read it and how access is granted.

limitations: Single MinIO node in v1 — no erasure coding, so the offsite mirror is the durability story.
There is no virus scanning in Phase 1; a ClamAV sidecar is planned if user uploads ever become publicly visible.
Presigned URL expiry is sensitive to clock skew between the API host and MinIO.
testFocus: Presigned PUT rejects an oversized or wrong-type upload
Verification catches a missing or mismatched object
Key generation is deterministic and idempotent
GC deletes orphans and never deletes a referenced object
Behaviour when MinIO is unavailable

decisions.question: Proxy uploads through the API or presign?
decisions.why: Proxying makes API memory and bandwidth scale with file size, which would cap horizontal scaling on the exact operation that grows fastest

decisions.question: MinIO or S3?
decisions.why: Self-hosted in v1 with no code change required to move to S3 later — the SDK and the semantics are the same

todo.title: Phase 1
items: Bucket definitions, policies and lifecycle rules
Per-bucket metrics and a disk alert

future: CDN in front of public buckets
Multi-node MinIO with erasure coding
Virus scanning for publicly visible uploads
doNot: Do not stream file bytes through a Go handler.
Do not make a bucket public without a review.
Do not generate a long-lived presigned URL.
Do not store a file reference before verifying the object exists.
Do not put personal data in an object key.

name: telemetry
purpose: OpenTelemetry setup and the middleware that makes every request, query, job and external call observable: tracer, meter and logger providers, resource attributes, propagation, correlation IDs, and the standard metric instruments.
context: This module ships in Phase 0 and is a prerequisite for everything else. Retrofitting observability costs several times what building it in does, and the first production incident is not the moment to discover you cannot see anything.
responsibilities: Tracer, meter and logger provider construction and shutdown
OTLP exporter configuration and resource attributes
HTTP middleware: trace context extraction, request ID, span naming, panic recovery
slog handler with the OTLP bridge and the PII redaction allowlist
Standard instruments (HTTP, DB, cache, storage, jobs) so modules do not each invent their own
Sampling configuration
Health and readiness endpoints
notResponsibilities: Running Prometheus, Loki, Tempo or Grafana — those are `deploy/`
Deciding what a module should measure — it provides the instruments, the module chooses

endpoints.purpose: Readiness — dependencies reachable and migrations current

contract.name: telemetry.Tracer
contract.purpose: Named tracer per module

contract.name: telemetry.Meter
contract.purpose: Named meter per module

contract.name: telemetry.Middleware
contract.purpose: The standard HTTP middleware chain

contract.name: telemetry.Instruments
contract.purpose: Pre-built histograms and counters shared by all modules

rules: The application exports only OTLP. Changing a backend is a Collector configuration change, never a code change.
Span names are low-cardinality — route patterns, never concrete IDs.
Metric labels are bounded: no user IDs, no free text, no unbounded identifiers. The budget is 10,000 series per metric.
Every log record is emitted through the redaction handler, which allowlists loggable attribute keys — a new key is redacted until explicitly permitted.
`trace_id`, `span_id` and `request_id` are attached by the middleware and the slog bridge, never by hand.
Sampling is decided in the Collector (tail-based) so a decision can see the whole trace.
`/ready` fails when a hard dependency is unreachable or the schema version is behind; `/health` reports only that the process is alive.
Shutdown flushes exporters before the process exits — a lost trace at shutdown is a lost incident clue.

flows.title: Correlation across a request and its background work
flows.mermaid:
flowchart LR A[Browser click
OTel Web SDK] -->|traceparent + X-Request-Id| B[API middleware] B --> C[root span] C --> D[slog records carry trace_id] C --> E[service span] E --> F[pgx span] E --> G[job enqueued with job.Meta
trace_id + request_id] G --> H[worker span links to the same trace] H --> I[ai span
provider, model, cost] D & F & I --> J[Grafana: log → trace → span → exemplar]

tasks.title: Instrument a new operation
steps: Start a span named `<module>.<Operation>` with `module` and `operation` attributes.
Record errors on the span with the `apperr` code, not the raw message.
Use an existing instrument if one fits; add a new one only if it does not.
Check label cardinality before adding a label.
Add a dashboard panel if this is a new user-facing capability, and an alert plus runbook if it can fail visibly.

limitations: Metric cardinality is enforced by review and a lint rule, not by the runtime — a careless label can still be shipped.
The browser SDK adds bundle weight and is loaded lazily after first paint.
There is no exemplar support from every instrument yet.
testFocus: Trace context propagates from HTTP through service, repository, job and AI call
The redaction handler blocks a non-allowlisted attribute
`/ready` fails correctly when Postgres or Redis is down
Shutdown flushes pending spans
Span names contain no IDs

decisions.question: Direct exporters or a Collector?
decisions.why: One ingest point; backend changes, sampling and redaction become operational configuration instead of a deploy

decisions.question: Jaeger or Tempo?
decisions.choice: Tempo in production, Jaeger only in the dev profile
decisions.why: Tempo shares MinIO for storage and integrates natively with Grafana; running both in production would double the operational surface for no benefit — see the plan review §6

decisions.question: zap/zerolog or slog?
decisions.why: Standard library, structured, and the performance difference is immaterial at our request volume

adrs.title: OTel SDK + Collector; Tempo over Jaeger

todo.title: Phase 0
items: OTLP exporters with resource attributes including version and commit
HTTP middleware: trace, request ID, recovery, structured access log
slog handler with the OTLP bridge and redaction allowlist
Standard instruments for HTTP, DB, cache, storage and jobs
Collector pipeline configuration including tail sampling
The first Grafana dashboard, proving log→trace correlation works

future: Continuous profiling with Pyroscope
RUM metrics from the browser SDK
Exemplars on all latency histograms
doNot: Do not put an ID in a span name or a metric label.
Do not add `trace_id` to a log record by hand.
Do not export directly to Prometheus or Tempo from application code.
Do not log a value whose key is not on the allowlist.
Do not skip instrumenting a new external call — it will be the one that fails.

name: mailer
purpose: Email transport: template rendering, localisation, sending through SMTP or a provider API, bounce and complaint handling, suppression lists, and a delivery log.
responsibilities: MJML/HTML template rendering with a plain-text alternative
Localisation of subject and body
Sending via SMTP or a provider API, behind one interface
Retry with backoff on transient failures
Bounce and complaint handling; suppression list
Delivery log for support and debugging
A development mailbox (Mailpit) so no real email leaves a developer machine
notResponsibilities: Deciding whether to send — that is `notification`

contract.name: mailer.Sender
contract.purpose: `Send(ctx, Message)` — always enqueues, never blocks the caller

contract.name: mailer.Message
contract.purpose: `{To, Template, Locale, Data, Category}`

consumes.name: user.deleted
consumes.reason: Purge the delivery log entries for that address

rules: Sending is always asynchronous — a mail provider outage must never fail a user request.
An address on the suppression list is never emailed, except for account-security messages, which bypass suppression only when the address is not a hard bounce.
Every template has a plain-text alternative and exists in every supported locale before it can be used.
Templates are rendered with escaping; user-supplied values are never interpolated as HTML.
Email addresses are logged as hashes; the delivery log stores `to_hash`, not the address.
Every non-security email includes a working unsubscribe link.
A hard bounce suppresses the address immediately; a soft bounce retries up to three times.
In development and CI, all mail is captured by Mailpit; a real send from a non-production environment is a configuration bug.

errors.meaning: Address is on the suppression list
Template missing for the requested locale

flows.title: Send with retry and suppression
flows.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Sender.Send(msg)"] --> B[enqueue email.send job]
    B --> C{suppressed?}
    C -->|yes, non-security| D[skip, log reason]
    C -->|no| E[render template + locale]
    E -->|template missing| F[fail loudly — this is a bug, not a runtime condition]
    E --> G[provider send]
    G -->|transient| H{attempts left?}
    H -->|yes| G
    H -->|no| I[log failed; alert if the category is critical]
    G -->|hard bounce| J[suppress address; publish email.bounced]
    G -->|accepted| K[log sent with provider message id]

tasks.title: Add an email template
steps: Create the MJML source and the plain-text alternative.
Add every supported locale — a missing locale is a startup validation failure, not a runtime fallback.
Add a preview fixture so the template renders in the dev mailbox with realistic data.
Test rendering with hostile input (HTML in a display name) to confirm escaping.
Add it to the notification category mapping if it is user-triggered.

limitations: No A/B testing or send-time optimisation for email; that logic, if it ever exists, belongs in `notification`.
Attachment size is capped at 10 MB; larger artefacts are delivered by presigned link instead.
Deliverability monitoring (SPF/DKIM/DMARC reporting) is manual.
testFocus: Suppression honoured for non-security categories and bypassed correctly for security ones
Retry classification: transient retries, hard bounce suppresses
Template rendering escapes hostile input
Every template exists in every locale (a startup validation test)
Webhook signature verification rejects a forged payload

decisions.question: SMTP or provider API?
decisions.why: SMTP works everywhere including local development; a provider API gives better deliverability signals in production. The choice becomes configuration

decisions.question: Template format?
decisions.why: Email HTML is a compatibility minefield; MJML solves it and the compile step keeps runtime rendering cheap

todo.title: Phase 1
items: Sender interface with SMTP implementation and Mailpit in dev
MJML build step and the first templates: verification, reset, new device

future: Provider API implementation
Deliverability dashboard
Per-template engagement metrics
doNot: Do not send synchronously from a request handler.
Do not log a raw email address.
Do not add a template without every locale and a plain-text alternative.
Do not interpolate user input into HTML without escaping.
Do not send real email from development or CI.

name: search
purpose: A thin abstraction over full-text search. Backed by PostgreSQL `tsvector` in v1, with an interface shaped so a dedicated engine can replace it without touching callers.
context: Deliberately minimal. Introducing Elasticsearch for a corpus of tens of thousands of items would add an operational dependency and a synchronisation problem to solve a query that Postgres answers in single-digit milliseconds.
responsibilities: Index definition and maintenance per searchable entity
Query building: tokenisation, prefix matching, ranking, highlighting
Reindex jobs, full and incremental
Language configuration for English content
Search latency and result-quality metrics
notResponsibilities: Owning the searchable data — each module owns its own rows and its own index
Semantic or vector search — that is `platform/ai` with pgvector

contract.name: search.Indexer
contract.purpose: `Index(ctx, doc)`, `Remove(ctx, id)` — called by the owning module on write

contract.name: search.Searcher
contract.purpose: `Search(ctx, Query) (Results, error)` with filters, ranking and highlighting

rules: The search index is derived data. It can always be rebuilt from the owning tables, and a rebuild must be routine, not an emergency.
Indexing happens in the same transaction as the write when it is a generated column, and via an event when it is a separate table.
Only published content is searchable by learners; admins may search drafts.
Every query is bounded by a `LIMIT` and returns a cursor.
Search must degrade to a simple `ILIKE` prefix match if the index is unavailable — a degraded search beats an error page.
Query latency above 300 ms p95 is the trigger to reconsider the backend, and is monitored for exactly that reason.

flows.title: Index maintenance
flows.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A[content.published] --> B[search job]
    B --> C[build tsvector from title, body, tags]
    C --> D[UPSERT into the module's search table]
    D --> E[GIN index]
    F[Learner query] --> G[normalise + tokenise]
    G --> H["websearch_to_tsquery + ts_rank"]
    H --> I[filter by level, skill, status]
    I --> J[highlight + paginate]

tasks.title: Make an entity searchable
steps: Add a `search_vector tsvector` generated column, or a dedicated search table if the document spans rows.
Add a GIN index.
Populate on write and on the relevant domain event.
Add a reindex job for backfill.
Add the entity to the search endpoint's type filter.
Measure p95 latency on realistic data volumes before shipping.

limitations: Postgres FTS has no built-in fuzzy matching beyond trigram similarity, no synonym management, and limited relevance tuning.
No cross-entity ranking — searching lessons and words together requires a union with hand-tuned weights.
Stemming is English-only; Vietnamese UI text is not full-text searchable.
testFocus: Ranking puts exact title matches first
Draft content is invisible to learners and visible to admins
Reindex produces the same results as incremental indexing
Degraded path when the index is missing
Query latency on a realistically sized dataset

decisions.question: Postgres FTS or a search engine?
decisions.why: Our corpus is small, our relevance needs are simple, and avoiding a second datastore avoids a synchronisation problem. The interface keeps the door open — and the p95 metric is the objective trigger to walk through it

decisions.question: Who owns the index?
decisions.choice: The module that owns the data
decisions.why: A central index would need to know every module's schema — precisely the coupling the architecture forbids

todo.title: Phase 4
items: tsvector generated columns and GIN indexes for content, vocabulary and question bank
Query builder with ranking, highlighting and filters
Latency metrics with the 300 ms p95 trigger alert

future: Trigram fuzzy matching for misspelled words
Synonym dictionary for vocabulary search
Semantic search over lessons via pgvector
A dedicated engine if the latency trigger fires
doNot: Do not add Elasticsearch without the latency trigger firing and an ADR.
Do not make the index a source of truth.
Do not run an unbounded search query.
Do not expose draft content to learners through search.
